explanations.answer: It is an abomination to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Moses gives, baker. The first husband may not remarry her after she has been defiled, "for that is an abomination to the LORD." Moses adds, "You must not bring sin upon the land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance." So the reason comes from the LORD Himself, not from a vote.

explanations.answer: Her second husband's family has a claim
explanations.explanation: Good guess, friend, but the text never mentions a claim from the second husband's family. Moses says the first husband may not remarry her, and his reason is that it is "an abomination to the LORD." He doesn't bring any family into it. Sometimes the answer is simply what the verse says, and this verse says it plainly.

explanations.answer: The elders must approve it first
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd reach for the elders, friend. They show up later in this very chapter. But in verse 4 Moses doesn't ask for approval. He says the first husband "may not remarry her," and he gives the reason: it is "an abomination to the LORD." No permission slip would change that.

explanations.answer: Stay home and bring joy to his wife
explanations.explanation: Yes! For one year he is free "to stay at home and bring joy to the wife he has married." No war and no duty, just home and his bride. I think that's a pretty sweet deal, friend, and I'd sign up for a year of that in a heartbeat.

explanations.answer: Serve the priests at the tabernacle
explanations.explanation: Serving the priests is a fine thing, friend, but it's not what Moses says. He calls it a year free from war and duty. That means no assignments at all, not even holy ones. The text says he is free to stay home and bring joy to his wife.

explanations.answer: Build a new house for his family
explanations.explanation: A new house sounds like a very responsible way to spend a year, baker. But Moses doesn't say a word about building. The man is "free to stay at home and bring joy to the wife he has married." The year is for her, not for a hammer.

explanations.answer: It would take his livelihood as security
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Moses says taking millstones "would be taking one's livelihood as security." The millstones are how he makes his daily bread. Imagine a lender walking off with my oven for a debt. I'd be sitting there with dough and a very sad face.

explanations.answer: Millstones belong to the whole town
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Moses never says the millstones belong to the town. His reason is that taking them "would be taking one's livelihood as security." The stones are the man's own tools for making a living. Take those away and he can't earn what he needs to pay the debt.

explanations.answer: They are too heavy to carry off
explanations.explanation: Ha! A millstone is no pocket item, friend, but weight isn't Moses' point. He says it "would be taking one's livelihood as security." The problem isn't carrying the stones. It's what the man loses when they're gone.

explanations.answer: Miriam
explanations.explanation: Yes, Miriam! Moses says, "Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam on the journey after you came out of Egypt." He brings her up right after the instructions about skin diseases. Miriam was Moses' sister, and her story is told in Numbers 12:10.

explanations.answer: Aaron
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, since Aaron, Moses' brother and Israel's high priest, was right there in that story (Numbers 12:10-11). But Moses names someone else in this verse. He says, "Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam." Her name is the one on the page.

explanations.answer: Korah
explanations.explanation: Korah, a Levite who rebelled against Moses (Numbers 16:1-3), is a different story, baker. That one isn't what Moses points to here. In this verse he tells Israel to remember what the LORD did "to Miriam on the journey after you came out of Egypt."

explanations.answer: So he can sleep in his own cloak
explanations.explanation: That's right. Moses says to return it by sunset "so that he may sleep in his own cloak and bless you." For a poor man, the cloak was what he had to sleep in. Nobody should have to spend the night cold while his neighbor holds the blanket.

explanations.answer: So he can work the next morning
explanations.explanation: Hard work matters, friend, but the text doesn't say that's the reason. Moses says the security must come back by sunset "so that he may sleep in his own cloak." The point is a night's sleep, not the next day's job.

explanations.answer: So he can repay the loan sooner
explanations.explanation: Nice thinking about the debt, baker, but Moses doesn't mention repayment here. He gives a different reason: "so that he may sleep in his own cloak and bless you." It's about the man's night, not his paperwork.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: True! Moses says, "this will be credited to you as righteousness before the LORD your God." Returning the cloak takes a few minutes and costs the lender nothing but a blanket. And the LORD counts it as righteousness. That's a good return, friend.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Moses really does say it: "this will be credited to you as righteousness before the LORD your God." That's said about returning the poor man's security by sunset. So the statement is true, and a little cloak carries a big word.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Moses says the opposite, friend. He says, "Do not oppress a hired hand who is poor and needy, whether he is a brother or a foreigner residing in one of your towns." So the protection covers Israelites and foreigners both. Nobody gets left off this list.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Right, baker! The protection isn't only for Israelites. Moses says a poor and needy hired hand is covered "whether he is a brother or a foreigner residing in one of your towns." Brother or foreigner, the rule is the same.

explanations.answer: Each day before sunset
explanations.explanation: Exactly. Moses says, "You are to pay his wages each day before sunset." Same day, no waiting. If I had to wait a week for my pay, I'd be eating crumbs off the counter by Wednesday.

explanations.answer: At the end of each week
explanations.explanation: A weekly paycheck is how plenty of people get paid today, baker. But Moses says something else here. He says, "You are to pay his wages each day before sunset." For this poor worker, pay comes the very same day.

explanations.answer: When the harvest is in
explanations.explanation: Waiting for the harvest would be a long wait, friend. Moses doesn't say that. He says, "You are to pay his wages each day before sunset." It's a daily payment, no waiting on the crops.

explanations.answer: He depends on it to get by
explanations.explanation: Yes. Moses says to pay him "because he is poor and depends on them." The wages are what he lives on. Holding them back isn't a small delay, it's taking from someone who has nothing to spare.

explanations.answer: He might quit for other work
explanations.explanation: That's a worry any boss might have, friend, but Moses doesn't say it. His reason is that the hired hand "is poor and depends on them." It's about the worker's need, not the master's convenience.

explanations.answer: His master might forget the debt
explanations.explanation: Forgetting is easy to do, baker. I once lost track of a whole batch while I was telling a story. But Moses doesn't give forgetfulness as the reason. He says the man "is poor and depends on them." The reason is his need.

explanations.answer: His own sin
explanations.explanation: That's it. Moses says, "each is to die for his own sin." Fathers aren't put to death for their children, and children aren't put to death for their fathers. Each person answers for his own.

explanations.answer: His father's sin
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Moses says, "Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers." A son doesn't pay for his father's sin. The verse says "each is to die for his own sin."

explanations.answer: His children's sin
explanations.explanation: Not this one, baker. A father isn't put to death for his children's sin. Moses says, "Fathers shall not be put to death for their children," and ends with "each is to die for his own sin." Everybody carries only their own.

explanations.answer: They were once slaves in Egypt
explanations.explanation: Yes! Moses says, "Remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you from that place. Therefore I am commanding you to do this." Israel knows what it's like to be on the low end, so they're to treat others with the same care they were shown.

explanations.answer: Foreigners bring trade to their towns
explanations.explanation: Trade is a smart angle, friend, but Moses never says it. His reason is, "Remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you from that place." The reason is their own history.

explanations.answer: Widows can take them to the elders
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a reason to behave, baker, but Moses doesn't say it here. He gives this one: "Remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you from that place." The reason is memory, not a threat.

explanations.answer: bless
explanations.explanation: Yes, bless. Moses says to leave the forgotten sheaf "so that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands." The sheaf you leave behind goes to the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow. I'd call that a very good way to lose a sheaf, friend.

explanations.answer: test
explanations.explanation: Close in sound, maybe, but not in the verse, friend. Moses says the LORD "may bless you in all the work of your hands." He doesn't say test. The forgotten sheaf is about blessing, not a pop quiz.

explanations.answer: judge
explanations.explanation: Not this time, baker. In this verse the LORD doesn't judge. Moses says He "may bless you in all the work of your hands." Leaving the sheaf behind is tied to blessing.

explanations.answer: So their brother isn't degraded
explanations.explanation: That's right. Moses says no more than forty lashes, "lest your brother be beaten any more than that and be degraded in your sight." Even a guilty man is still called your brother. The limit protects his dignity.

explanations.answer: So the judge can hear more cases
explanations.explanation: A busy judge is a believable idea, friend, but Moses doesn't say it. The cap is there "lest your brother be beaten any more than that and be degraded in your sight." The reason is the man himself, not the court schedule.

explanations.answer: So the punishment ends by sunset
explanations.explanation: Sunset does come up in this chapter, baker, but not here. In verse 3, Moses says the limit is "lest your brother be beaten any more than that and be degraded in your sight." Nothing about the clock.

explanations.answer: Muzzle it
explanations.explanation: Yes. Moses says, "Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain." The ox is working the grain, so it's not shut out from it. I'd say that's a fair deal for a hard worker, friend.

explanations.answer: Yoke it with a donkey
explanations.explanation: That's a different law, friend. In Deuteronomy 22:10, Moses says not to plow with an ox and a donkey together. Here the rule about the ox treading grain is simpler: "Do not muzzle an ox."

explanations.answer: Sell it to a foreigner
explanations.explanation: Nothing about selling in this verse, baker. Moses says only, "Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain." The law is about how the ox is treated while it works.

explanations.answer: So his name isn't blotted out from Israel
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. Moses says the first son "will carry on the name of the dead brother, so that his name will not be blotted out from Israel." The brother is gone, but his name keeps going through that son.

explanations.answer: So the widow can keep her husband's house
explanations.explanation: A house is a sensible thing to worry about, friend, but the text doesn't mention one here. Moses says the first son will carry on the dead brother's name "so that his name will not be blotted out from Israel."

explanations.answer: So the elders can count him in the tribe
explanations.explanation: The elders do appear in this passage, baker, but not for this reason. Moses says the son carries the name "so that his name will not be blotted out from Israel." Counting the tribe isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: He refuses to preserve his brother's name
explanations.explanation: Yes. She says, "My husband's brother refuses to preserve his brother's name in Israel. He is not willing to perform the duty of a brother-in-law for me." She brings her case to the elders at the city gate, where they handled matters like this.

explanations.answer: He has taken her husband's field
explanations.explanation: Land disputes are real, friend, but that isn't her complaint here. She tells the elders, "My husband's brother refuses to preserve his brother's name in Israel." It's about the name, not a field.

explanations.answer: He won't let her glean his harvest
explanations.explanation: Gleaning is in this passage, baker, but it's in Deuteronomy 24 and not part of this complaint. At the gate she says, "My husband's brother refuses to preserve his brother's name in Israel." That's her whole case.

explanations.answer: This is for the man who won't keep his brother's line
explanations.explanation: Right. She declares, "This is what is done to the man who will not maintain his brother's line." That's after the elders have spoken with him and he still says he doesn't want to marry her. It's a hard moment, baker.

explanations.answer: This is for the man who took his brother's land
explanations.explanation: Land isn't part of this, friend. Her words are, "This is what is done to the man who will not maintain his brother's line." It's about the family line, not a property fight.

explanations.answer: This is for the man who broke his word to the elders
explanations.explanation: The elders are standing right there, baker, so I see why you'd think it. But the widow doesn't say he broke his word. She declares, "This is what is done to the man who will not maintain his brother's line."

explanations.answer: So they may live long in the land
explanations.explanation: Yes. Moses says to keep honest weights and measures "so that you may live long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you." Honest scales and a long life in the land go together in this verse, friend.

explanations.answer: So the priests get a fair tithe
explanations.explanation: Fair is a good word, baker, but the tithe isn't what Moses mentions. He says honest weights and measures are for this: "so that you may live long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you."

explanations.answer: So the king can tax them fairly
explanations.explanation: Taxes would sure be a modern reason, friend! But Moses doesn't mention a king or taxes here. He says, "so that you may live long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you."

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: True. Moses says, "For everyone who behaves dishonestly in regard to these things is detestable to the LORD your God." He means the weights and measures. A crooked scoop isn't a small thing to Him, baker.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Moses says it plainly: "For everyone who behaves dishonestly in regard to these things is detestable to the LORD your God." So the statement is true. Honest dealing matters.

explanations.answer: The stragglers at the back
explanations.explanation: Yes. Moses says the Amalekites "attacked all your stragglers." Israel was "tired and weary," and the ones at the back got hit. I think that makes the story hard to hear, friend.

explanations.answer: The priests carrying the ark
explanations.explanation: The priests and the ark are not in this verse, baker. Moses says the Amalekites "attacked all your stragglers." The ones hit were the ones lagging behind.

explanations.answer: The leaders at the front
explanations.explanation: Not the front, friend. Moses says they came at the people "when you were tired and weary, and they attacked all your stragglers." The ones at the back were the ones in danger.

explanations.answer: fear
explanations.explanation: Yes, fear. Moses says of the Amalekites, "they had no fear of God." So he's naming that as part of what they did when they attacked Israel's tired stragglers.

explanations.answer: love
explanations.explanation: Love is a big word, friend, but it isn't the word in this verse. Moses says the Amalekites "had no fear of God." Fear is the one.

explanations.answer: word
explanations.explanation: Not word, baker. The verse says the Amalekites "had no fear of God." That's the phrase Moses uses about the ones who attacked Israel's stragglers.
